title: Kernel density estimation
sub: One bump per point; the bandwidth decides how smooth the result is.

frames.caption: 30 data points (orange ticks) drawn from some unknown distribution. Kernel density estimation guesses that distribution without assuming its shape.
Put a small Gaussian bump on every point (each with area 1/30). The bandwidth h = 0.4 is the bumps' width.
Add the bumps up. That sum (blue) is the density estimate: tall where points crowd together, low where they are sparse.
Too narrow (h = 0.08): a spike on every point. It memorizes the sample; held-out data scores badly (high variance). Held-out log-likelihood -4.456.
Too wide (h = 1.6): the two groups blur into one lump (high bias). Held-out log-likelihood -1.997.

Silverman's rule of thumb, h = 1.06·σ̂·n<sup>−1/5</sup> = 0.85: close to the true density (dashed). It assumes roughly bell-shaped data, so with two groups it smooths a little too much; h = 0.4 scored slightly better on held-out data, which is why cross-validation is the more careful choice. Held-out log-likelihood -1.806.
